She was treated with antibiotics and recovered well with no myasthenic complications.

The patient died of cardiac arrest, thought to be secondary to her malignancy . She presented with persistent hypotension of unclear source and required 2 pressors . CT of the abdomen showed a large mass in the right lobe of her liver, with possible peritoneal and lymph node involvement . Hematology/oncology felt she had incurable disease with a grim prognosis, with no possible treatment option .

The patient is on Coumadin because CT angiogram showed a small blood clot in one of the vessels serving the lungs (pulmonary embolus). Blood thinners lovenox and coumadin were started to address the lung clot, with treatment recommended for 3-6 months. CT torso showed no evidence of right cardiac abnormalities. The patient developed shortness of breath in the context of fever and immobility, prompting the CT angiogram that revealed the pulmonary embolus.

Based on the medical record, the patient's kidneys will not recover. Renal consultation determined that the patient would require chronic hemodialysis . The patient tolerated hemodialysis well, with stable blood pressure and no muscle cramping . Outpatient dialysis was arranged three times weekly . Discharge instructions explicitly state the patient will need to continue going to dialysis three times a week , indicating permanent dialysis dependency.

The patient died following complications from acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, GI bleed, and acute on chronic kidney injury. He developed a hypotensive episode likely due to gastrointestinal hemorrhage with persistent BRBPR requiring multiple blood transfusions. Volume overload from left heart failure and steroid therapy was managed with continuous veno-venous hemodialysis. Following recurrent GI bleed, rigid scope revealed ischemic colitis but he was a poor operative candidate. Given grim prognosis, he was made comfort measures only.

The bleeding from the mouth and nose was caused by an upper GI bleed from variceal bleed (bleeding esophageal varices). An emergent endoscopy with banding was performed in the ICU. The patient was resuscitated with blood products (4 pRBCs, 2 platelets, 1 FFP) and given IV PPI and octreotide drip for 48 hours, as well as 5 days of IV ceftriaxone. The patient was stabilized, though continued to have melena.

The patient developed ventricular tachycardia during hospitalization, which can be a life threatening heart rhythm. The patient was discharged home with a lifevest which is worn externally and will shock if this dangerous rhythm occurs again. Additionally, Metoprolol succinate was started as a new medication to help take some of the work load off the heart and lower heart rate and blood pressure.

Post-operatively, the patient awoke neurologically intact but required Precedex for extubation. Postoperative confusion and agitation was treated with Haldol and Zyprexa, all narcotics were discontinued. He remained in the CVICU until his mental status improved. Psychiatry and social work were consulted to evaluate postoperative confusion with hallucinations. His mental status returned to baseline by POD#9, when he was cleared for discharge to home with Visiting Nurse services.

The patient has an anoxic brain injury after a PEA arrest during a VT ablation procedure. CT head shows stable reduction in gray-white differentiation. EEG shows mild to moderate encephalopathy with no epileptiform discharges or electrographic seizures. He has a tracheostomy and PEG tube. The tongue laceration occurred from biting; total teeth extraction was performed. He is being treated for MRSA bacteremia with vancomycin and possible aspiration pneumonia. Discharge disposition is extended care facility.

The patient was initially treated with levofloxacin and Unasyn to cover for aspiration and community-acquired pneumonia. Coverage was broadened to vancomycin/Zosyn on hospital day 3. After completing a week of antibiotics, she remained persistently febrile with negative cultures. Antibiotics were then held. The patient is currently being treated with multi-drug therapy for presumed pleural tuberculosis. Fever has improved since induction of TB therapy.

The patient's intracerebral hemorrhage was treated conservatively with blood pressure control and monitoring. He was offered a Factor VII trial but refused, and there were no other alternative therapies indicated. His BP was initially controlled with a labetalol drip for a goal SBP <140 in the neuro ICU, and aspirin and heparin products were held. Repeat imaging showed the hemorrhage was stable. He was then transferred to the floor where BP medications were titrated.

The acute renal failure likely started from poor forward flow from initial cardiogenic failure and was probably exacerbated by 320 ccs of contrast received in the cath lab. She developed muddy brown casts on urine analysis. Due to hyperkalemia to 6.8 and anuria immediately post cath, she was treated with CVVHD. She is likely now dialysis-dependent with oliguria, however renal consultants believe she continues to have potential to regain renal function.

The patient had an exploratory laparotomy for necrotic uterus with abscess, developed polymicrobial sepsis with bacteremia, then required second surgery for perforated diverticulitis with pelvic peritonitis requiring colon resection and colostomy placement. At discharge, the patient was doing well, afebrile with stable vital signs, tolerating regular diet, ambulating with assistance, with decreasing white blood cell count on intravenous antibiotics. Patient was discharged to rehab for continued recovery.

The patient's pain was well controlled with Percocet (oxycodone-acetaminophen 5-325 mg). At discharge, she was prescribed 1-2 tablets every 4-6 hours as needed for pain, to be taken with food. She was also given acetaminophen 325 mg, two tablets every 4-6 hours as needed. The discharge instructions specified not to take Percocet with Ativan (lorazepam).

The bleeding gums in this patient were caused by thrombocytopenia (low platelet count). The patient had several reasons for low platelets: end-stage liver disease (ESLD), splenomegaly, critical illness, and multiple antibiotics that are reversibly myelosuppressive. The bleeding diathesis was related to the platelet count rather than elevated INR. Aminocaproic acid was used for gum bleeding. There is no mention of oral cancer concerns in this excerpt.
